Allah, may He be exalted, pointed to these in His saying: ﴿and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, by their inability, humiliation and grief, as they see their palms being cut down and burned while they have no means of repelling it.

In any case, the permission to fight, which involves the shedding of blood, the taking of lives, and what follows from it of captivity and spoils, does not prevent, in a case like the cutting of palms, if the matter requires it. It may be said that what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted is, by the permission of Allah, permitted.

On this basis it may be said: when Muslims besiege an enemy and see that it is in their interest, or in the humiliation of the enemy, to destroy his installations and property, there is no prohibition against that, and Allah knows best.

The most that can be said is that it is the destruction of part of the property in order to prevail over the enemy and seize all of his property. This has a parallel in the Sharia, such as the action of al-Khidr with the ship of the poor people when he damaged it, that is, he made it defective by destroying part of it, so that he could save it from the usurpation of the king. He said: ﴿and I did it not on my own accord﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

The objection of the polytheists to the Muslims concerning their fighting in the sacred months came about, just as the Jews objected to the Muslims about cutting the palms. This is in His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great (sin), but barring from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, and (barring from) al-Masjid al-Haram, and expelling its people from it, is greater with Allah; and fitnah is greater than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

The polytheists magnified the killing by Muslims of some polytheists at the Battle of Nakhlah, and they had not verified that the sacred month had begun, and they accused them of transgressing the sanctity of the sacred months. So Allah answered them according to what they had said, that fighting in the sacred month is great, but what the polytheists committed of barring from the way of Allah, disbelief in Allah, barring from al-Masjid al-Haram, and expelling its people from it, who were the Muslims, is greater with Allah; and fitnah against the religion is greater than killing, that is, what they denounced from the Muslims.

Likewise here: if the Jews magnified the Muslims' cutting of some palms and found fault with the Muslims for causing corruption by destroying some property, then how about their treachery and betrayal, their breaking of covenants, and their conspiring to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Ka'b ibn Malik recorded this meaning, mentioning the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir and the killing of Ibn al-Ashraf:

"Indeed the Jews were disgraced by their treachery, as the turning of time goes round with its changes.

And that is because they disbelieved in a Lord whose command is great and mighty.

And they had been given, together, understanding and knowledge, and there came to them a warner from Allah."

Until he said:

"When they were soaked in treachery and disbelief, and aversion from the truth turned them away,

Allah showed the Prophet, with a sound opinion, and Allah judges and does not wrong,

So He strengthened him and gave him power over them, and He was a helper to him, the best of helpers."

He indicated that the disgrace of Banu al-Nadir was because of their treachery and their disbelief in their Lord. So the permission to cut the palms was a legal permission, and it may be said of it that it is a legislative action when the need calls for it, just as the need called for it here. And Allah knows best.

The pronoun in (مِنهم) here refers to the Banu al-Nadir.

*Fay'* (spoils obtained without battle) is booty taken without fighting. Allah here made it specific to His Messenger.

He said: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur any horse or camel for it, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. That is, since the expulsion of the Jews was attributed to Allah, the Most High, through the terror He cast into their hearts, and through His having given His Messenger (ﷺ) power over them, this fay' belonged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, and no one else shared in it.

The confirmation of this comes from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him). The Shaykh, may Allah shower him with His mercy, cited it at the end of his discussion of the topics of *al-Anfal*, at his words: "Ninth issue: know that «he (ﷺ) used to take the sustenance of his year from the fay' of the Banu al-Nadir, not from the ghanima (war booty).»" He cited the hadith of Anas ibn Aws, agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning the matter of ʿAli and al-ʿAbbas demanding their inheritance from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) said to them: "Indeed Allah had specified His Messenger (ﷺ) in this matter with something He did not give to anyone else." Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur for it...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿...All-Powerful﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. "So it was exclusively for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). By Allah, he did not take it to the exclusion of you, nor did he monopolize it over you. He gave it to you and distributed it among you, until this wealth remained from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to spend on his family from this wealth the sustenance of his year, and then take what remained and place it in the place of what belongs to Allah, etc." [End of quotation.]

This was specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but after it came something more general in His saying: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the traveler﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. That is, in general terms.

Because this verse is general both in its source and in its disbursement, it contains many rulings and numerous issues. The Shaykh, may Allah shower him with His mercy, had already discussed everything in it at the beginning of *Surat al-Anfal*, at His saying: ﴿They ask you about the al-Anfal﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. He comprehensively and thoroughly explained and clarified the sources and disbursements of fay' and ghanima and nafl (voluntary extra gift), and the lands conquered by peaceful treaty or by force, and many issues beyond which nothing more is needed and from which no one can dispense. And all praise is due to Allah, the Most High.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 59, verse 7 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿So that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you.﴾

The meaning of *al-dulah* and *al-dawlah*, with a *damma* on the *dal* in the first and a *fatha* in the second, revolves among the exegetes around two meanings. *Al-dawlah* with a *fatha* means victory in war and other things, and it is the verbal noun. With a *damma*, it is the name of the thing that is passed around among wealth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of the verse is: "So that the *fai'* (property taken from the enemy without fighting), which is rightfully to be given to the poor so that it becomes their sustenance by which they live, does not become a thing that circulates among the rich, who multiply it among themselves." Or it means: "So that it does not become a *dawlah* of the *jahiliyyah* (pre-Islamic age of ignorance) among them."

The meaning of the *dawlah* of the *jahiliyyah* is that their leaders used to monopolize the spoils, because they were the people of leadership, dominance and power, and they used to say: "Whoever is mighty takes the spoil." The meaning is: "So that its taking by force does not become a selfish practice of the *jahiliyyah*." From this is the saying of al-Hasan: "They made the servants of God a means of service, and the wealth of God a circulating commodity," meaning that whoever overpowered others among them took it and monopolized it, etc.

What is worth mentioning here is that the advocates of some corrupt economic doctrines argue from this verse in support of their corrupt doctrine, and say: "It is permissible for the state to seize the sources of production and the capital, in order to give them to the poor or to make the poor partners in them, whom they call the working class." This, despite the economic decline and social corruption it has caused, has been proven wrong, and its falsehood has become evident, and it departs from the reality of the argument.

This is because this wealth is left for the general public interests of the Muslims, such as spending on the mujahideen and securing the raiders at the borders and frontiers, and it is not given to individuals as they claim. Furthermore, it is essentially wealth that came as spoils for the Muslims, and it is not the result of an individual's labour and earning.

Since the spoils are not the property of a particular person, nor are they the earnings of a specific individual, generality is realised in their source, which is the spoils, and generality in their expenditure, which is the general interests of the Ummah. The individual has no share in them and no existence within them. How vast is the difference between this principle in legislation and this branch used for misguidance!

It is regrettable that they support their claim by inserting into it the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "People are partners in three things: water, fire and pasture." It is known that partnership in these three things, as long as it remains in its generality, means that water is shared by all as long as it is at its source in the river, the public well, the rain-flood or the pool. However, if it is moved from its public source and comes into the possession of someone, no one has a share in it with the one who possesses it. For example, whoever fills a vessel from the river or the flood or the like, what is in his vessel belongs exclusively to him. Likewise, this pasture, as long as it is grass on public land and not in the ownership of a specific person, is common to whoever reaches it first. When a person mows it and takes possession of it, no one has a share in it. Similarly, what grows on a person's own property is more entitled to him than others.

This becomes clear with fish in the sea and the river, which are common to all, and birds in the air, which are hunted. This is a shared portion among all hunters. When a person hunts it, he has taken possession of it and it becomes his exclusively. This is a matter that all economic systems recognise, and official licences are issued for it.

There is also the practice that prevails in those states, which makes them contradict their claim of partnership in water, fire and pasture. This is the case with water and electricity companies. They place in every house a meter that counts the gallons of water consumed by the household and charges them for it. If they fall behind in payment, they cut off the water and deprive them of drinking it.

Likewise, electric current is fire, and it is the most effective energy in cities. They measure it with a meter that counts kilowatts and sell it to the consumer. So why do they not make water and electricity a partnership among the citizens? Or are people partners only in what does not return to the state, while the state's right is exclusive to the rulers? This is the exact opposite of the case of the *fai'*.

Since the *fai'* and the spoils, which God has made lawful from the enemy's property, are a general earning that entered the Ummah through the effort of the whole Ummah, embodied in the army that fights in its name, God, the Exalted, placed them in general channels of the Ummah's interests:

﴿For God and for the Messenger, and for the near of kin, the orphans, the needy and the traveller.﴾

﴿For God﴾: that is, for jihad in the way of God.

﴿And for the Messenger﴾: for his carrying out of the affairs of the Ummah. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to take the annual maintenance of his household, and he would return what remained to the way of God.

﴿And for the near of kin﴾: those whose maintenance is obligatory upon him.

﴿The orphans and the needy﴾: this is social solidarity within the Ummah.

﴿And the traveller﴾: the one cut off on his journey, and this is a guarantee for communications.

Its expenditure was thus, by this generality, without being restricted to a particular person or group: ﴿So that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you.﴾

It is indeed among the places of miraculous eloquence in the Qur'an that after this legislation comes the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it, and fear God﴾ [al-Hashr: 7] and the rest of the verse. This is because it is legislation on a matter that touches the sensitive nerve in the soul, which is the place of stinginess and greed, namely the earning of wealth, which is the twin of the soul. God took upon Himself the distribution of a more important matter than this, which is inheritance.

He distributed it, the Exalted, explaining its obligations and the share of each heir, because it is an earning without equivalent, and a compulsory earning. Souls are eager for it, so God took charge of it. Likewise the *fai'* and the spoils, and He forbade embezzlement (*ghulul*) of them before their distribution.

This kind of wealth is the one they were accustomed to having distributed as spoils, and for which they had sacrificed their lives and their souls before reaching it. Then they find themselves prevented from it, and a barrier is placed between them and it, so that only movable property is distributed and fixed real estate is not distributed. It is said to them: "This has happened, so that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you," whether the rich are rich by their bodies and their ability to work and to fight, or rich by their wealth, having acquired spoils before that.

It was inevitable that their souls would move towards this wealth, and indeed they debated with 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, about it. But here comes the whip of obedience, drawn, and the decisive command of legislation: it is from God, that the Messenger of God brought to you: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it, and fear God﴾. Although this verse is general in all legislation, here it is more specific, closer to this matter, and the context more in need of it.

Here our discussion moves to what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought to us concerning this very meaning, namely the meaning of sharing in wealth.

When he (ﷺ) came to Madinah, the Ansar (the Helpers) preferred the Muhajirun (the Emigrants) over themselves, even though they themselves were in need. God had helped them to overcome the stinginess of their souls. Their society was a society of giving, generosity, sacrifice (p. 35) and preference for others. Yet it happened that a guest would come to him (ﷺ) and he would find no hospitality in his house. He would say to his companions: "Who will host this one tonight, and he will have Paradise?" One of his companions would take him. And the poor Muhajirun would come to him asking for something to mount them for jihad, and he would apologise to them that he had nothing to mount them on. They would turn away with their eyes overflowing with tears from grief that they could not find anything to mount them on. A cup of milk would be brought to him, and he would call out: "O people of the Suffah (the Ahl al-Suffah)!" so that they could share it with him, because of the scarcity of what they had. Abu Hurayrah would go out of the mosque and fall down at its door from hunger, while many of his companions were wealthy. Among them was one who equipped an army from his own wealth, and among them was one who gave away a whole caravan with everything in it, and among them was one who gave away the best orchards of Madinah. And among them, ... none of them ever took, not even one dirham, from whoever gave away a whole caravan with what it carried; he did not take from him a single dirham without his consent, so that one of the people of the Suffah might share it with him. Nor from whoever gave away his orchard did he take a sa' of dates to give to Abu Hurayrah to ease his hunger, nor a single camel from whoever equipped an army from his own wealth to carry a volunteer on it in the way of God.

These are honoured wealths and stable properties belonging exclusively to their owners. There is spoil and *fai'* which was taken by the strength and support of the Ummah for the army, placed in general channels for the Ummah and the army. Here, however, are private properties that were not touched or handled except with the consent of the soul and the goodwill of the heart. That is why they gave generously and did not withhold, they bestowed and did not hoard, they preferred others over themselves even though they themselves were in need. It was a society of mutual support, harmony and compassion. A further clarification of this society will come when we speak of the society of Madinah at God's saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ [al-Hashr: 8], and what follows of the verses, God willing.

The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, has a convincing discussion on this question in Surah al-Zukhruf at God's saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32] and the rest of the verse. We quote his text for its importance:

He, may God have mercy on him, said: "Issue: This noble verse mentioned here, and similarly God's saying, 'We have distributed among them their livelihood,' and God's saying, 'God has favoured some of you over others in provision' [al-Nahl: 71], and similar verses, indicate that the disparity among people in provisions and fortunes is one of God's heavenly, cosmic, decreed laws (*sunan*), which none of the people of the earth can at all change or alter in any way: ﴿So you will not find any change in the way of God, nor will you find any alteration in the way of God﴾ [Fatir: 43]. By this it becomes established that what the atheists today, who deny the existence of God and all the heavenly prophecies and messages, use as a pretext for extorting the people's wealth and stripping them of their private property, under the claim of equality among people in their livelihoods, is a false matter that is not possible under any circumstances. Yet they do not really intend what they claim; rather, they intend to monopolise the properties of all people, so that they may enjoy them and dispose of them as they wish, under a thick veil of lies, delusion and deception, as every intelligent person who knows their conduct and their situation with society in their countries realises.

So the small ruling clique and whoever joins them are the ones who enjoy all the good things of the country, while the rest of the common people are deprived of every good, wronged in everything, even of what they have earned with their own hands. They are fed with a ration card, as mules and donkeys are fed.

God, the Majestic and Exalted, knew in His eternal knowledge that there would come people who would usurp the people's wealth on the pretext that this one is poor and that one is rich. God, the Majestic and Exalted, has forbidden following desires under that pretext, and has threatened whoever does not desist from that with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them. So do not follow desire, lest you deviate. And if you distort or refuse, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Aware﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. And in His saying: ﴿Indeed God is ever, of what you do, Aware﴾ is a severe warning to whoever does that. End of verbatim quote."

The truth is that provisions are the distribution of the Creator. He is more compassionate to His servants than they are to themselves, and there is no deficiency in His treasuries. Rather, it is wisdom for the benefit of His servants. In the sacred hadith: "Among My servants is one for whom poverty is suitable; if I made him rich, his condition would be corrupted. And among My servants is one for whom wealth is suitable; if I made him poor, his condition would be corrupted." So He, glorified is He, gives according to measure, and does not withhold out of stinginess.

For this context, the sequence of the noble verse that the Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—discussed in its style is sufficient, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have apportioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 32]. This pronoun is known to be for magnification and exaltation, and likewise the pronoun in "apportioned" (qasamna). There is no room for the interference of created beings, and no place for anyone other than Allah, Exalted is He, in this matter. When the apportioning is from Allah, Exalted is He, no power on earth can overturn it. Moreover, the reality of life confirms this, and indeed depends upon it, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 32].

These transgressors against people's wealth acknowledge this, and affirm the system of classes, workers and non-workers, etc. So there is no evidence in the verse of Surat al-Hashr here: ﴿So that it does not become a perpetual circulation among the rich among you﴾ (p-37), and they have no right to what they did to people's wealth on the basis of this false principle. And Allah, Exalted is He, knows best.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾.

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him, Exalted is He—said in the introduction: The entire Sunnah is included under this noble verse, i.e., it is binding upon the Muslims to act upon the prophetic Sunnah, so taking up the Sunnah is taking up the Book of Allah. The confirmation of this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [An-Najm: 3–4].

Al-Suyuti said: Revelation is of two kinds:
A revelation we were commanded to write down and were worshipped by reciting, and that is the Noble Qur'an.
And a revelation we were not commanded to write down, nor were we worshipped by reciting, and that is the Sunnah.

The predecessors and successors of this Ummah have acted accordingly, as reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said in his session in the Prophet's Mosque: "Allah has cursed, in His Book, the woman who joins (her hair) and the one who has it joined, and the woman who tattoos and the one who has herself tattooed." A woman standing near him said: "And in the Book of Allah?" He said: "Yes." She said: "I have read it from its cover to its cover, and I did not find what you say." He said to her: "Had you read it, you would have found it, or did you not read His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the woman who joins and the one who has it joined, and whoever the Messenger of Allah has cursed, Allah has cursed." She said to him: "Perhaps some of your family do it?" He said to her: "Enter and look." So she entered his house, then came out and said nothing. He said to her: "What did you see?" She said: "Good," and departed.

Al-Shafi'i came and stood among the people of Makkah and said: "Ask me, O people of Makkah, about whatever you wish, and I will answer you from the Book of Allah." A man asked him about the muhrim who kills a hornet, what is upon him in the Book of Allah? He said: Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs," the hadith... "and so-and-so narrated to me from so-and-so," and he traced his chain back to Umar ibn al-Khattab, who was asked: "What is upon the muhrim who kills a hornet?" He said: "There is nothing upon him."

Thus Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab considered the Sunnah to be from the Book of Allah, and al-Shafi'i considered the Sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs to be from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is from the Qur'an. Each of them considered his answer to be from the Book of Allah, based on this noble verse.

(p-38) This is what the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) hold: they use it to specify the generality of the Book and to restrict its absolute terms.

Of the first kind: his ﷺ saying: "Two dead animals and two bloods have been made lawful for us: as for the two dead animals, they are locusts and fish; as for the two bloods, they are liver and spleen." By this hadith he specified the generality of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 3]. Likewise in marriage: "A woman shall not be married while her paternal aunt is (married to him), nor a woman while her maternal aunt is," and by it was specified the generality of: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [An-Nisa': 24], and similar examples are many.

Of the second kind: his ﷺ cutting off the hand of the thief from the wrist, as a restriction of the absolute: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 38]. Likewise, wiping the two palms in tayammum, as a restriction or clarification of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6]. Similar examples are many. Likewise is the clarification of the mujmal (general, unspecified) as the clarification of the mujmal in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 43]. He did not specify the number of rak'ahs for each time, nor the manner of performance, so he ﷺ prayed upon the minbar while they watched, then said to them: "Pray as you have seen me pray," and performed Hajj and said to them: "Take from me your rites."

They have agreed that the Sunnah consists of sayings, actions, and tacit approval (taqrir). His saying, Exalted is He, has made acting upon actions obligatory: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 21]. Emulation (ta'assi) includes both saying and action, but it is stronger in action. Tacit approval is included within action, since it is the abstaining from denouncing a matter, and abstaining is an action according to the usuliyyun, as the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud said:

"Abstaining is an act, according to the sound opinion."

* *

Note
His actions ﷺ are divided into several categories:

First: what he did by natural disposition (jibillah), which is the requirements of life, such as eating, drinking, dressing, and sleeping. All of this he did in response to the requirements of life, and he used to do it before the mission, and every person does it. So it is on the original permissibility (ibahah al-asliyyah), and there is no new legislation in it. However, the form of the act and its manner, such as eating and drinking with the right hand, etc., and it being from in front of the eater, is the locus of emulating him ﷺ. Likewise the type of food, or his abstaining from it, unless there is an impediment, such as his not eating dhabb (a lizard) and cooked greens; he explained the reason for this: the first, because it was not in the land of his people, so he disliked it; the second, because he converses with One whom we do not converse with. The author of Maraqi said:

"And his action established in the natural disposition, like eating and drinking, is not heedless (of the attribute) without noticing the attribute..."

(p-39)

Second: what was ambiguous between natural disposition and legislation, such as his ﷺ standing at Arafat riding his she-camel, and his descending at al-Muhassab when departing from Mina. The standing, which is the pillar of Hajj, is completed by being present at the place of standing at Arafat in any state. So was his standing while mounted part of the completion of his rite, or did he do it without intending a rite? This is a disagreement among the usuliyyun. And it is not far-fetched to say: his action ﷺ may have been to make himself more visible in such a gathering, to facilitate for whoever wished to ask a question, see him, or have a need; so it would be legislation for one who holds his position of responsibility.

Third: what was established as specific to him, such as the permissibility of his combining more than four wives in marriage, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 50], and they were more than four; and marrying a woman who gives herself to him, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A privilege for you, excluding the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 50]. For this, no one shares with him.

Fourth: what was an explanation of a Qur'anic text, such as his ﷺ cutting off the hand of the thief from the wrist, as an explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 38], and like the rites of Hajj and prayer, which are an explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 43], and His saying: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾ [Al-Imran: 97]. Therefore he ﷺ said: "Pray as you have seen me pray," and said: "Take from me your rites." This category's ruling for the Ummah is the ruling of what is explained (mubayyan): so in obligation it is obligatory, and in other matters, according to its degree.

Fifth: what he ﷺ did neither by natural disposition nor as explanation, and whose specificity to him was not established. This is of two types. One: that his ruling in relation to the Messenger ﷺ is known, whether obligatory, recommended, or permissible, so its ruling for the Ummah is likewise, like his ﷺ prayer inside the Ka'bah; we know that it is permissible for him ﷺ, so for the Ummah it is permissible. Second: that his ruling in relation to him ﷺ is not known. In this category there are four opinions:

The first: obligation, acting on the safer course. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, some Shafi'is, and a narration from Ahmad.

The second: recommendation, because the act is preferred over abandoning it. This is the view of some Shafi'is, and also a narration from Ahmad.

(p-40) The third: permissibility, because it is the certain (minimum). But this applies only to what has no act of devotion in it, since acts of devotion are not described as merely permissible.

The fourth: suspension (tawaqquf), because the intended meaning is not known. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah, and this is the weakest of the opinions, because suspension involves no emulation.

From these four opinions it follows for us that the sound position is to perform the act in emulation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as obligatory or recommended. They illustrated this act with his ﷺ removing his sandals during prayer, and all the Companions removed their sandals. When he ﷺ finished, he asked them about their removing their sandals. They said: "We saw you do it, so we did it." He said to them: "Jibril came to me and informed me that there was filth on my sandals, so I removed them." So he approved of their removal in emulation of him, and did not blame them, even though they did not know the ruling before he informed them. And here there has come what you say, in the form of generality.

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said, in removing the misconception concerning Surat al-Anfal, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [Al-Anfal: 24], the following text: This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that responding to the Messenger, which is obeying him, is obligatory only when he calls us to what gives us life. A parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will not disobey you in what is right﴾.

And there has come in other verses what indicates the obligation of following him absolutely, without any condition, such as His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [Al-Hashr: 7].

And His saying: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ (the verse) [Al-Imran: 31], and ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa': 80].

The apparent reconciliation, and Allah knows best, is that the verses of absoluteness make clear that he ﷺ calls us only to what gives us life, of the good of this world and the Hereafter. So the condition stated in His saying: ﴿when he calls you﴾ is fulfilled in the call of the Prophet ﷺ because of his infallibility, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [An-Najm: 3–4].

The conclusion: the verse ﴿when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ makes clear that there is no obedience except to one who calls to what pleases Allah, and the other verses made clear that the Prophet ﷺ never calls except to that. May the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him (p-41). Ended.

The Sunnah has also clarified the reality and the ultimate scope of what he ﷺ brought, in his saying: "I have not left any good that brings you closer to Allah except that I have explained it to you and commanded you to it, and I have not left any evil that distances you from Allah except that I have explained it to you, warned you against it, and forbidden you from it."

* *

Note
In reality, acting upon this noble verse is a necessary consequence of a Muslim's pronouncing the two testimonies. For his saying, "I bear witness that there is no deity except Allah," is an acknowledgment to Allah, Exalted is He, of divinity and its necessary implications, among which is sending Messengers to His creation and sending down His Books. And his saying, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," is an acknowledgment of Muhammad's ﷺ messengership from Allah to His creation. This necessitates taking up everything that this Noble Messenger brought from Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He. It is not permissible to worship Allah except in what the Messenger of Allah brought, nor is it right for him to disobey Allah in what the Messenger of Allah has forbidden. Thus it is, in truth, a requirement of pronouncing the two testimonies.

This is supported by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [An-Nisa': 59], where He linked the referral of disputes to Allah and the Messenger with belief in Allah and the Last Day.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 59, verse 7 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding this verse in "Surat al-Nisa'": In this noble verse, Allah commands that whatever people dispute concerning the fundamentals of the religion (usul al-din) and its branches (furu'ihi), the dispute over it must be referred back to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 80]. End of quote.

From all of this it becomes clear that what the Prophet ﷺ brought us is from Allah, and that it holds the same status as the Qur'an in legislation (al-tashri', the making of law), and that the Sunnah is independent in legislating, as it came with the prohibition of the flesh of domestic donkeys, every animal with a claw among birds and a fang among beasts of prey, and the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt, or with her brother's daughter or her sister's daughter, and similar matters. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I will not find any one of you reclining on the couch of his household, saying: 'We only follow what we find in the Book of Allah; what we do not find in it, we leave.' Beware, I have been given the Book and its like along with it."

The text here is general (al-nass 'amm) in taking whatever has been brought to us and in abandoning what has been forbidden to us. This generality ('umum) has been specified (takhsis) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286],
• and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ [an-Nur: 61],
• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286].

The hadith also distinguished between the generality of the prohibition and the command, in His ﷺ saying: "What I have commanded you, do of it what you are able; and what I have forbidden you, avoid it." This concluding phrase (al-tadhyil) on this verse came in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], signifying (iydhanan) that this obligation admits no leniency, that it binds the Ummah both privately and publicly, and that whoever opposes any part of it is addressed by this severe warning, because disobeying it is disobedience to Allah, and obeying it is obedience to Allah: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab) (p. 414):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Hashr

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾.

The aspect of reconciling the unrestricted (al-itlaq) in this verse with the restriction (al-taqyid) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when He calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will not disobey you in what is right﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12], has already been discussed (p. 41) in Surat al-Anfal.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 59, verse 8 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾

In this noble verse there is a comprehensive description of the emigrants regarding the motives of the emigration, that they: ﴿seek bounty from Allah and His pleasure﴾; and its goal, which is: ﴿and support Allah and His Messenger﴾; and the judgment for them, that: ﴿those are the truthful.﴾

The explicit meaning of these attributes indicates by its implicit meaning (mafhum) that they are specific to the emigrants. However, other texts indicate that the Helpers (al-Ansar) shared in this with them, among them His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and support - those are allies of one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], and His saying after it: ﴿And those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and support - those are the believers in truth﴾ [al-Anfal: 74].

He mentioned the emigrants with striving by wealth and self, and mentioned with them the Helpers with sheltering and support, and described both groups together with the allegiance of some of them to others, and established for them together the reality of faith: "Those are the believers in truth," i.e., the truthful in their faith. So the Helpers were equal to the emigrants in the factor of support and in the truthfulness of faith.

And in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them and do not find in their breasts any need for what they (the emigrants) were given, and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾ (p-43) [al-Hashr: 9], is a comprehensive description of the Helpers. ﴿Had settled in the abode﴾ means Madinah; ﴿and in faith before them﴾ means the first and second Pledge of al-'Aqabah before the coming of the emigrants, and even before the faith of some of the emigrants. ﴿They love those who emigrate to them﴾ and receive them with open breasts; ﴿and they prefer﴾ others ﴿over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾, because the emigrants had come to them.

The apparent meaning of the texts indicates by its implicit meaning that others did not share in these qualities with them. But in the first verse there is what indicates that the emigrants shared with the Helpers in this noble attribute, which is preference over oneself (al-ithar), because the true reality of preference over oneself is giving wealth to another in his need while placing the other above oneself. This very meaning had already been found among the emigrants themselves, as stated in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties﴾ [al-Hashr: 8]. They had homes, they had wealth, and they were expelled from all of it. So if the Helpers consoled their emigrant brothers with some of their wealth and shared their possessions with them, the emigrants did not merely give up some of their wealth, but left it all: their wealth, their homes, their children, and their families. They became poor after being expelled from their homes and properties. Whoever leaves all his wealth and home, and abandons his family and children, is no less in sacrifice than one who prefers another with some of his wealth while remaining settled in his family and home. So it is as if Allah compensated them through this fay' for what they had lost.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ said to the Helpers something that conveys this meaning, namely his saying ﷺ: "Indeed your brothers have left behind their wealth and children and have come out to you." They said: "O Messenger of Allah! Our wealth between us is in shares..." the hadith.

That is, the Helpers recognized this for the emigrants, and acted upon it. Thus the emigrants were equal to the Helpers in this ideal, noble attribute, and it became a character trait of many of them after the Hijrah, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) did when he gave away all his wealth, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "What have you left for your family?" He said, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have left for them Allah and His Messenger." Likewise 'A'ishah al-Siddiqah (may Allah be pleased with her), when she was fasting and had nothing but a loaf of barley, and a beggar came, and she said to Barirah: "Give him what you have." Barirah said to her: "There is nothing but what you will break your fast with." She said: "Give it to him; perhaps she needed it more at that moment," or as she said.

When evening came, a goat's leg was sent to them as a gift, wrapped in its qiram. Its qiram is what the Arabs used to do when they wanted to roast a goat: they would coat it from the outside with dough to protect it from the ash of the embers (p-44). She said to Barirah: "Eat, this is better than your loaf."

Likewise 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him) gave in charity the caravan and what it carried of merchandise when it arrived, while the Messenger ﷺ was delivering the Friday sermon, and the people went out to it.

On this basis, the society of Madinah in the time of the Prophet ﷺ was a society of mutual solidarity, some of them allies of others. The Prophet ﷺ, in the matter of the spoils of Hunayn, emphasized the virtue of both groups in his saying ﷺ: "Were it not for the Hijrah, I would have been a man of the Ansar."

And after him 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I enjoin the caliph after me regarding the first emigrants, that he recognize their right and preserve their dignity. And I enjoin him regarding the Ansar, good, those who settled in the abode and in faith, before that: that he accept the good-doers among them and overlook their wrong-doers."

Then this was the character of the emigrants and the Helpers together, as occurred at the battle of al-Yarmuk. Hudhayfah al-'Adawi said: "I set out on the day of al-Yarmuk seeking a cousin of mine, and with me was some water, and I was saying: if he has any breath left, I will give him drink. Then I found him, and I said to him: Shall I give you drink? He gestured with his head that yes. Then I heard a man saying: Ah, ah. My cousin gestured to me to go to him. It was Hisham ibn al-'As. I said: Shall I give you drink? He gestured that yes. Then he heard another saying: Ah, ah. Hisham gestured to me to go to him, so I came to him and found that he had died. I returned to Hisham and found that he too had died. I returned to my cousin and found that he too had died."

And the method of the elite after them was as al-Qurtubi related from Abu Yazid al-Bistami, who said: "No one ever overcame me as a young man from the people of Balkh overcame me. He came to us as a pilgrim and said to me: What is the limit of asceticism (zuhd) among you? I said: If we find, we eat; and if we lack, we are patient. He said: This is how the dogs of Balkh are with us. I said: And what is the limit of asceticism among you? He said: If we lack, we give thanks; and if we find, we prefer others."

Regarding His saying: ﴿and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾, al-ithar 'ala al-nafs (preference over oneself) is putting others before oneself while in need. And al-khasasah (privation) is that by which the condition is disrupted; its root is from al-ikhtisas, which is being alone in a matter. So al-khasasah is being alone with need, i.e., even if they had poverty and need. From it is the poet's saying:

"As for spring, when there is privation, the sick person lives by it, and the needy becomes rich."

(p-45) Is preference over oneself valid for every person, even if he has dependents or is obliged to support others, or not? And what is its relation to His saying: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]?

The answer to all this is in the words of the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, on His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. In this noble verse He expressed with min (from) of partition, indicating that one spends for the sake of Allah part of what he has, not all of it. Here He did not explain the amount that should be spent and the amount that should be kept. But He explained in other places that the amount that should be spent is the excess beyond need and the filling of the necessary deficiency, as in His saying: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾. By al-'afw (surplus) is meant what exceeds the amount of necessary need, according to the most correct interpretations, and this is the view of the majority. From it is His saying: ﴿until they multiplied ('afaw)﴾ [al-A'raf: 95], i.e., they increased, and their wealth and children increased.

Some scholars said: al-'afw is the opposite of al-juhd (exertion), namely that one spends what does not reach the point of exertion and exhausting of capacity.

From it is the poet's saying:

"Take the surplus from me, and your affection will endure, and do not speak in my anger when I am angry."

This saying returns to what we mentioned, and the remaining sayings are weak. His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29] forbids stinginess by His saying: ﴿do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, and forbids extravagance by His saying: ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, so the middle course between the two is determined, as He explained by His saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither wasteful nor stingy, but are between that a moderate stance﴾ [al-Furqan: 67].

Therefore the spender must distinguish between generosity and squandering, and between stinginess and niggardliness. Generosity is other than squandering, and moderation is other than stinginess. Withholding where giving is required is blameworthy, and Allah forbade it to His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. Giving where withholding is required is also blameworthy, and Allah forbade it to His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾.

(p-46) The poet has said:

"Do not praise the son of 'Ibad, even if his hands pour like clouds, until he shames the rain. For those are impulses of his whisperings: he gives and withholds, neither out of stinginess nor out of generosity."

Allah, may He be exalted, explained in other places that praiseworthy spending is not so unless its disbursement is in what pleases Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend, it is for parents and the nearest kin﴾ 1 the verse [al-Baqarah: 215]. He also stated that spending in what does not please Allah is a regret for its owner, in His saying: ﴿So they will spend it, then it will be a regret for them﴾ the verse [al-Anfal: 36].

The poet has said:

"Indeed a favor is not a favor until the path of the one who makes it is struck by it."

If it is said: what you have established implies that praiseworthy spending is spending of what exceeds necessary need, yet Allah praised a people for spending while they themselves were in need of what they spent. This is in His saying: ﴿and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

The apparent answer, and Allah knows best, is what some scholars mentioned: that every situation has its own speech. In some circumstances preference over oneself is prohibited, such as when the spender has obligatory expenses, like the maintenance of wives and the like, and he spends voluntarily on what is not obligatory and abandons the duty, in accordance with the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Begin with those whom you support." Or such as when he has no patience to refrain from asking people, so he spends his wealth and then goes to people asking for their wealth; it is not permissible for him to do so. Preference over oneself is valid when he has not neglected an obligatory expense, and he is confident in himself regarding patience, chastity, and not asking.

As for the view that His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ means zakat, the matter is clear, and knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted. End of his words.

The reality is that spending in the Qur'an has three levels:

The first: spending from part of one's wealth in a general manner, as in His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾.

(p-47) The second: spending from what a person loves and is keen upon, as in His saying: ﴿and gives wealth despite love for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and this is more specific than the first, and His saying: ﴿and they feed, despite love for it, the poor, the orphan, and the captive﴾ the verse [al-Insan: 8].

The third: spending together with preference over oneself, like this verse: ﴿and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾. This is more specific than the first specific category.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 59, verse 8 (part 2 of 2):

The first rank is considered the minimum floor of what is obligatory. It was said that it refers to zakat (obligatory almsgiving). It also includes voluntary charity (nafilah), and it applies to the least amount, even half a date. It falls under His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7]. The third rank is considered the maximum limit, because it is preference of others over one's own personal needs (ithar). The second rank is the middle between them. It is the middle limit between being content with the least of what is obligatory and preferring others over oneself. It is the standard of moderation for the general population, as Allah, exalted is He, explained with His statement: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. Likewise, Allah, exalted is He, praised a people for moderation in His statement: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that moderate﴾ [al-Furqan: 67].

This is exactly the application of the rule of moral philosophy (al-falsafah al-akhlaqiyyah) which states: virtue is a mean between two extremes, namely the extremes of excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit). For example, courage is a mean between recklessness and cowardice, and generosity is a mean between wastefulness and stinginess.

Spending has multiple aspects and varying rulings. The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, explained one aspect of the rulings, and the Qur'an has explained the other aspects. They are limited to the following: the type of what is spent, the recipient of the spending, the attitude of the spender, and the form of spending.

As for what is spent: Allah, exalted is He, first specified that it is from lawful earnings, by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not intend the defective therefrom to spend, while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook in it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267].

And His statement: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 92].

As for the recipient of the spending: it is as in His statement: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say, "Whatever wealth you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215]. So He began with the parents, as an act of kindness to them, and then mentioned the relatives.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity given to a relative is both charity and maintaining family ties; charity given to a distant person is only charity." Then (the verse mentions) orphans. This is a human duty and social solidarity (takaful ijtima'i), because the orphan of today is the spender of tomorrow, and the child of parents today may become an orphan tomorrow. That is, whoever is kind to an orphan today may leave orphans behind, and that orphan whom you were kind to yesterday will be kind to them. "The needy, and the traveler" are general matters.

He brought the general rule by which Allah, exalted is He, holds accountable and rewards its doer: ﴿And whatever good you do﴾, that is, in absolute terms, indeed Allah is Knowing of it [al-Baqarah: 215]. His knowledge, exalted is He, is sufficient in this regard.

As for the attitude of the spender and the form of spending: this is the secret of spending in Islam, and the entire philosophy of spending appears in this aspect. In this respect Islam is distinguished from all other religions or systems.

Because it focuses on preserving the feelings and sensitivity of the needy, so that one does not make him feel the wound of poverty or the humiliation of need, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminder or injury—for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 262].

Then He preferred a good word over harmful charity in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need and Forbearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 263], that is, one gives and does not reproach for the gift.

He made clear to the spenders that reminding and injuring nullify charity: ﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reminders or injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], because of what it contains of wounding the feelings of the needy.

He also urged concealing it, going to great lengths to preserve his feelings and sensitivity: "If you disclose your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you" (﴿If you disclose the charities, then they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾) [al-Baqarah: 271], that is, along with the earlier etiquettes, "it is better for you": that is, for yourselves, in preserving their reward.

The Prophet (ﷺ) counted among the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade on the Day when there is no shade but His: "A man who gave charity and concealed it, until his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent." And as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and publicly, will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274].

(p-٤٩) Among the distinctive features of Islam in this domain is that just as it disciplined the rich in the manner of spending, it also disciplined the poor in the manner of receiving. This is in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿For the poor who are restricted in the way of Allah and cannot move about in the land. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you will recognize them by their mark. They do not ask people persistently﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 59, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

The Qur'anic text: ﴿O you who believe, fear God, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow. And fear God; indeed God is Acquainted with what you do.﴾.

In this noble verse there is an exhortation to God-consciousness (taqwa) in general, and it is coupled with an exhortation to reflect and consider what every soul has sent forward for tomorrow. The command to fear God is repeated in it, which indicates the intensity of concern and care for taqwa, as will be explained in detail, God willing, whether the repetition is for emphasis (ta'kid) or for establishing a new meaning (ta'sis). Its explanation will come, God willing.

As for the concern with exhorting to taqwa, several verses of the Book of God attest to it. Even if it were said that the purpose of the whole message of Islam, and indeed of all religions, is the attainment of taqwa, it would not be far-fetched. This is for the following reasons:

First: God's saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may attain taqwa﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 21]. It is known that God did not create jinn and humankind except to worship Him, so taqwa, by the meaning of these two verses, is the purpose of creating the two weighty ones, humankind and jinn. The text has come in detail concerning each nation separately. Among them, concerning the people of Noah, peace be upon him, God said: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers. When their brother Noah said to them, "Will you not fear God? Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger. So fear God and obey me."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 105–108]. Concerning the people of 'Ad, God said: ﴿'Ad denied the messengers. When their brother Hud said to them, "Will you not fear God? Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger. So fear God and obey me."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 123–126]. Concerning the people of Lot: ﴿The people of Lot denied the messengers. When their brother Lot said to them, "Will you not fear God? Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger. So fear God and obey me."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 160–163]. Concerning the people of Shu'ayb, God's saying: ﴿The companions of the thicket denied the messengers. When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not fear God? Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger. So fear God and obey me."﴾ (p-50) [Ash-Shu'ara: 176–179].

So every prophet called his people to taqwa, as we have mentioned. Then the whole Qur'an came as a call to taqwa and as guidance for the God-conscious (muttaqun), as at the beginning of the noble Qur'an: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 1–2]. It explained the type of this guidance, which includes the meaning of taqwa, in God's saying: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them. And who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is those who are the successful﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 3–5].

The Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon him, explained the meaning of taqwa at God's saying: ﴿But righteousness is in one who fears God﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 189]. He said: "He did not explain here who the muttaqi is, and God has explained it in His saying: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; and who establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise; and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the muttaqun﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177]."

Several verses have also shown the effects of taqwa in this world and in the next. Among its effects in this world is God's saying: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾ [At-Talaq: 4]; His saying: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [At-Talaq: 2–3]; His saying: ﴿And fear God; and God teaches you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 282]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [An-Nahl: 128].

As for the next life and the Hereafter, taqwa accompanies its possessor from the start to the gates of Paradise, as in God's saying: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide eternally"﴾ [Az-Zumar: 73]. When they enter it, it unites them, renews their bonds among themselves, and makes them feel secure from every fear, as in God's saying: ﴿Friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the muttaqun. "O My servants, no fear will be upon you this Day, nor will you grieve. Those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims. Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted."﴾ (p-51) up to His saying: ﴿For you therein is fruit in abundance from which you will eat﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 67–73]. This continues until it brings them to the highest 'Illiyyun, and settles them in a seat of truth, as in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, the muttaqun will be in gardens and rivers, in a seat of truth, in the presence of an all-powerful King﴾ [Al-Qamar: 54–55].

Thus, by all of this, the station of taqwa in Islamic legislation, and in every heavenly law, becomes clear. Here it is in the context of exhorting to it and repeating it. The poet made it the complete happiness, as in his words, which are by Jarir:

"I do not consider happiness to be the gathering of wealth, but the God-fearing one is the happy one."

"The fear of God is the best provision as a store, and with God is increase for the most God-conscious."

Taqwa is always the impetus for every good and the restraint from every evil. Ibn Kathir narrated in his tafsir from Imam Ahmad: "When a group from Mudar came, wearing wraps of cloth and cloaks, barefoot and naked, with swords slung on them, the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ changed color. He entered, then came out, and commanded Bilal to call to prayer. He prayed, then delivered a sermon to the people, reciting God's saying: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul﴾ [An-Nisa: 1] to the end of the verse, and he recited the verse in the surah of 'Al-Hashr': ﴿O you who believe, fear God, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow﴾ [Al-Hashr: 18]. A man gave charity from his dinar, from his dirham, from his garment, from a sa' of his wheat, from a sa' of his dates, until he said, 'even with half a date.' Then a man from the Ansar came with a purse his hand almost could not hold; rather, it could not hold it. Then the people followed one another until I saw two heaps of food and clothing, until I saw the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ glowing as if it were gilded. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it after him, without any of their rewards being diminished.'" So taqwa was the impetus for establishing a good practice, at which the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ glowed.

Just as it prevents evil, of this is God's saying: ﴿And let the one who has the obligation dictate, and let him fear God, his Lord, and not leave anything out of it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 282], and His saying: ﴿And let the one who has been entrusted discharge his trust and fear God, his Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 283]. Indeed, taqwa prevents the denial of rights and the loss of trusts. Similarly is His saying about Mary, concerning her purity and chastity, when Gabriel came to her and appeared to her as a well-proportioned man: ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing"﴾ [Maryam: 18].

(p-52) And as in the hadith of the three men whom the cave shelter sheltered, among them the man with his cousin, when she said to him, "Fear God, and do not break the seal except by right," so he got up from her and left her the wealth.

Likewise it is in the conduct of the servant, as in God's saying: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of God, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [Al-Hajj: 32].

The address in God's saying: ﴿And let every soul look﴾ [Al-Hashr: 18] is to every soul, as in God's saying: ﴿Then every soul will be compensated for what it earned﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 281], and His saying: ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 25].

So the call to taqwa comes first, addressing the specific believers, and the command to reflect addresses the general population of every soul. This is because those who benefit from taqwa are specifically the believers, as the Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon him, clarified at the beginning of Surat Al-Baqarah. Reflection, however, is required of every soul. So the specific is for compassion (al-ishfaq), and the general is for warning (al-tahdhir).

The first is indicated by God's saying: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 43].

The second is indicated by His saying: ﴿The Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a great distance. And God warns you of Himself, and God is Kind to [His] servants﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 30]. And what is in God's saying: "what it has sent forward" is general, covering good and evil, and small and great.

The first is also indicated by God's saying: ﴿The Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a great distance﴾.

The second is indicated by God's saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Az-Zalzalah: 7–8], and the hadith: "Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date."

"Ghadan" (tomorrow) is applied to the future as opposed to the past, as the poet said:

"I know the knowledge of today and yesterday before it, but I am blind to the knowledge of what is in tomorrow."

Most of its usages in the Qur'an are according to this, such as God's saying about the brothers of Joseph: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow; he will frolic and play﴾ [Yusuf: 12], and His saying: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, unless God wills"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 23–24].

(p-53) It is also applied to the Day of Resurrection, as here in this verse, because the Qur'an indicates that. Of this is God's saying in the same meaning: ﴿The Day a man will look upon what his hands have sent forward, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [An-Naba': 40].

The contextual indicators in the verse include: its being framed by an exhortation to fear God both before and after it.

Among them is the concluding warning in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, God is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Al-Hashr: 18], meaning: with the intentions in deeds, and with the outward and the inward. And because the Day of Resurrection is a place of forgetting, it needed to be drawn to attention.

Referring to the Day of Resurrection as "tomorrow" is due to its nearness of coming and the certainty of its occurrence, as in God's saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ [Al-Qamar: 1], and His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or it is even nearer. Indeed, God is over all things competent﴾ [An-Nahl: 77].

From another angle, "tomorrow" for each person in the sense of the Day of Resurrection is realized on the day of his death, because he witnesses what he has sent forward on the day of his death. The words "soul" and "tomorrow" are indefinite here: the first is said to be for the few who look, and the second for the greatness of its matter and the severity of its terror.

Here the command to fear God has been repeated twice, as we have stated earlier. It has been said that this is for emphasis (ta'kid), as Ibn Kathir said, and it has been said that it is for establishing a new meaning (ta'sis), as al-Zamakhshari and others said.

Now, on the view that it is for emphasis, it is clear. On the view that it is for establishing a new meaning, the first would be for performing the commanded act, and the second for abstaining from the forbidden, supported by the first being followed by the requirement of action, "and let every soul look to what it has sent forward," and the second being followed by the requirement of warning, "Indeed, God is Acquainted with what you do."

Although this has a valid basis, and the view of emphasis is supported by God's saying: ﴿Fear God as He should be feared﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 102], and although that ruling was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun: 16], its meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿And others who have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad﴾ [At-Tawbah: 102], meaning: by neglecting some of what is commanded and doing some of what is forbidden.

Accordingly, taqwa is not realized except by observing both sides. However, the root of taqwa, which is taking a shield against what brings God's punishment, encompasses both matters together in the law, by His saying in the general command to take a shield: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ (p-54) [At-Tahrim: 6].

So one of the two commands to taqwa suffices for that and encompasses it, and the second command to taqwa is for a new meaning. The verse points to it, namely God's saying: "what it has sent forward," because "what" is general, as we have stated, and the form "has sent forward" is in the past tense. So the command to fear God first concerns what has passed and what preceded of deeds already done, and looking refers to accountability and reflection, in the sense of the hadith: "Hold yourselves accountable before you are held accountable." Ibn Kathir mentioned it.

When one looks back at the past, takes account of oneself, and recognizes what shortcomings or transgressions one has committed, the second command comes: to have taqwa of Allah regarding the new deeds one will undertake in the future, and to be aware that Allah is watching over him: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 234]. Thus there is no repetition and no division of meaning. Rather, the meaning follows the general sense of "mā" and the past form "qaddamat" (it has sent forward), and "the looking" is for the purpose of self-reckoning.
